prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of GLP-1 and the identification of its active form, which made incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: I keep B033 as a single-part prize with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and I did not change my configuration after the first round. The round-1 record shows the same scientific case in all six statements, and it is a case about the discovery: incretin physiology and secretion in humans (Holst), the receptor biology and the intestinotropic and metabolic actions that supplied the therapeutic rationale (Drucker), and the biologically active GLP-1(7-36) peptide (Mojsov). That chain explains why degradation-resistant agonists work, and independent outcome trials on glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal endpoints leave maturity beyond dispute. The chair's observation is that round 2 turns on attribution and on whether a second part is wanted, not on merit. On the second question I still say no. The GLP-1 part already uses all three names, no member prefers a pairing, and none of B039, B036, B018 or B004 has a defensible attribution that would justify diluting a prize whose core is settled. The citation should keep the physiology and the active form as the achievement and mention the therapeutic consequence only as its result.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakness and I cannot resolve it from the supplied files. Mojsov's priority for the active truncated peptide is contested, Habener and Bell are outside the credited list, and Knudsen, who led the development of liraglutide and semaglutide, is left out by the three-person cap, so the prize can be read as honouring the hormone and not the medicines. If the committee were to conclude that the priority for the active form cannot be defended, the fallback I would accept is Drucker and Holst with Mojsov replaced by Knudsen, not a silent substitution, and I would want that stated openly. Separately, long-term safety and durability of the obesity benefit are still being characterised, though I agree with El-Manira that this does not change the case.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius argued that Holst and Drucker are secure whichever way the Mojsov and Habener question is settled, asked for the attribution evidence on GLP-1(7-36) to be examined explicitly, and would reconsider Knudsen only if Mojsov cannot be defended.
responses.response: I agree that two of three names do not depend on the dispute, and that is the main reason I am comfortable going into the vote with the trio. I also support your request that the chair make the priority question for the active peptide an explicit item, but I should be honest that the supplied files do not let me settle it, and neither of us should claim otherwise. I accept your fallback: if the committee judges Mojsov's claim indefensible, Knudsen is the strongest replacement, and I would not extend the prize to Habener, who is not on the credit list. Where I stay with my position is that a contested but plausible claim to the active form is not enough to drop her, since the identification of GLP-1(7-36) is the step that made the hormone concept therapeutically coherent.

responses.point: El-Manira would want the committee to test a Holst and Drucker pair before deciding on Mojsov, and judges that durability of the obesity benefit does not change the case.
responses.response: Testing the pair is a reasonable discipline. A Holst and Drucker prize would be secure on attribution, but it would leave out the identification of the active peptide, which is the link between the physiology and why the agonists work, and the citation would then have to be written around a gap. I therefore prefer the trio, and I would only move to the pair if the evidence on priority turned against Mojsov, not merely because it is disputed. On durability I now agree with you and have softened my earlier hesitation: the effect on weight and cardiorenal outcomes has held across several drug classes and trials, so I treat durability as a continuing question for the field, not a reason to wait.

responses.point: Linnarsson regards Knudsen as the most natural omission under the cap, would limit B039 to June and Sadelain, and wrote that the optogenetics attribution needs a clearly defensible set before it can pass.
responses.response: I accept your point on optogenetics, and it moves me. In round 1 I ranked B018 second for its effect on causal neuroscience. With six credited names, Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck all holding claims, and direct clinical use limited to early retinal work, I cannot propose three names that I could defend, so it stays only as a late alternative and I would not pair it with B033. On Knudsen, I agree the cap is not a verdict that industrial development matters less. Where I differ slightly is that I would let the citation carry the therapeutic consequence rather than rely on the narrative alone, as the chair's second question suggests.

responses.point: Perlmann argued that Knudsen's analogues are the translation step, that the discovery trio can carry the therapeutic arc through citation wording, and that B039 would be a later or second-part candidate, not a challenger to B033 this year.
responses.response: I agree on all three points, and the citation I propose follows your wording suggestion: the achievement is the physiology and active form, and incretin-based therapy is named as what it made possible. I also agree that B039 is not a rival to B033 this year. Solid-tumour limits, toxicity and manufacturing leave CAR-T less settled than incretin therapy, which is a fair maturity comparison. I would add that the Eshhar gap matters more to me than the Rosenberg question, so if B039 is ever the lead part, the citation and the decision to proceed would both need to address it.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, asked whether Knudsen should be recognised within the prize, and treated B039 as the second candidate, with June and Sadelain acceptable as a two-person part.
responses.response: On the chair's question, I do not want Knudsen recognised within this prize at the cost of Holst or Drucker, since I see no principled way to remove either, and I agree with Wahren-Herlenius that a separate part or a different year would be more honest than trading away a discovery scientist. I would not use a second part to rescue her, because the cap would make that configuration worse for both parts. On B039, I agree a June and Sadelain pair is more faithful to the CAR achievement than adding Rosenberg, but it is an alternative for me and not a second part this year.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 form can be defended. I cannot verify it from the supplied files and am relying on recollection, as are several colleagues.
How the absence of Habener, Bell and other early proglucagon contributors from the credit list should affect the allocation, if at all.
Whether the committee will accept recognising the discovery scientists and not the industrial developer (Knudsen), which the three-person cap forces and which some will read as unfair.
Whether a later year would suit a B039 prize, given Eshhar's absence from the credited names and the open question of Rosenberg.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have co-authored with Linnarsson, a fellow committee member, and with Frisén's group at Karolinska Institutet. None of the credited names on the shortlist (Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen and the others) is a documented collaborator, mentor or institutional colleague. My field of single-cell and RNA biology is not the field of any shortlisted achievement, and I do not infer ties from shared topics. I note that I am more sympathetic to methods than my vote shows, and I have tried not to let that inflate B018.
